197.title: Who's the greatest? (Mark 9:30–37)
197.hook: they argue about rank; he puts a child in the middle
197.carry: last of all, servant of all
197.howItsDone: Many churches have deacons, a word from the Greek for servant, who care for the poor and help at worship, and Christians often point to this passage when talking about leadership as service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father at the foot of the mountain prayed with belief and doubt in one breath. Your line was help my unbelief. Did you bring the half you had? Day one hundred ninety-seven.

Picture a long car ride with kids in the back seat, and a muttered fight going on the whole way. You pull in at home, turn around, and ask: what were you arguing about back there? Silence. Everyone suddenly fascinated by the window. That's this scene. Jesus is walking through Galilee quietly, and for the second time he tells his friends that he'll be handed over and killed, and rise after three days. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask. Then they reach the house in Capernaum, and he asks them what they were arguing about on the road. And Mark tells us, in the King James Bible: "But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed among themselves, who should be the greatest."
screen: `A SECOND WARNING ON THE ROAD.` → `WHAT WERE YOU ARGUING ABOUT?` → `SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Notice the timing. He has just told them he's going to suffer and die, and they spend the walk arguing about who's number one. Mark doesn't soften it. Jesus doesn't shout, either. He sits down, the way a teacher did when about to teach, calls the twelve over, and says: "If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all." The Greek word for servant is diakonos, the one who waits on tables. It's where the church later got the word deacon. So the ladder is turned upside down. The way up is the way down. The greatest is the one bringing the plates. Then he does something they'll never forget. He takes a child, stands the child right in the middle of the circle of grown men, and takes the child up in his arms. And he says: whoever welcomes one little child like this in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. In that world, children were loved but had no standing at all. They couldn't vote on anything, own anything, or repay a favor. So welcoming a child is welcoming someone who can do nothing for your rank. That's the point. Churches today still wrestle with this one, in different ways: who gets the seat at the front, who serves the coffee, who is noticed. The argument on the road is very old, and very ordinary. And his answer is sitting right there in the middle of the room, in his arms.
screen: `ARGUING ABOUT RANK ON THE WAY.` · `LAST OF ALL, SERVANT OF ALL.` · `DIAKONOS: THE ONE WHO WAITS TABLES.` · `A CHILD IN THE MIDDLE.` · then, large: `THE SAME SHALL BE LAST OF ALL, AND SERVANT OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the youngest person in your day. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone younger than you whom you'll see today. A child, a grandchild, a student, a new person at work, the youngest in the family chat. Picture them clearly. What would serving them look like? Listening to the whole long story. Making them something. Asking their opinion and meaning it. Choose one thing. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Who's the greatest? The argument on the road. His answer: the last of all, the servant of all, and a child in the middle.
Your line: last of all, servant of all. Today, do the one thing you chose for someone younger, and don't mention it to anyone. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

198.title: Not one of us (Mark 9:38–41)
198.hook: whoever is not against us is for us
198.howItsDone: Many churches take part each January in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, when Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant congregations pray together or visit one another, and this passage is among those often read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples argued about rank, and he stood a child in the middle. Your line was last of all, servant of all. Who did you serve, quietly? Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Every group has its unofficial rules about who's in. The right jersey. The right school. The group chat you were or weren't added to. Now, just after the lesson about the child, John speaks up. John is one of the inner three, and Mark has told us Jesus nicknamed him and his brother the sons of thunder. He has news, and you can hear that he's pleased with it. In the King James Bible: "Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us." A stranger, doing good, using the name of Jesus. And they shut him down. Listen to the reason, twice over. Not: he doesn't follow you. He doesn't follow us.
screen: `WHO'S IN THE GROUP?` → `A STRANGER, USING THE NAME.` → `HE FOLLOWETH NOT US.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers in two words: "Forbid him not." Nobody, he says, who does a mighty work in my name can turn around the next moment and speak evil of me. And then the line: "For he that is not against us is on our part." The circle is wider than John drew it. Anyone working on the same side counts, even without the membership card. And then he makes it smaller still: whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you belong to Christ, will not lose their reward. A cup of water. That's the bar. The Hebrew Bible has a scene like this. In the book of Numbers, two men named Eldad and Medad start prophesying in the camp without having been at the official gathering, and young Joshua begs Moses to stop them. Moses says, in effect: I wish all the Lord's people were prophets. To be fair, the Gospels also keep a saying that sounds like the opposite. In Matthew, Jesus says whoever is not with me is against me. Christians hold both. Many read the one in Matthew as about where a person stands toward Jesus himself, and today's as about how his followers treat people outside their own circle. There are thousands of churches today, and Christians argue about real things. But many churches also join each year in a week of prayer for Christian unity, and this passage is one they often read. The disciples' question was who's with us. His answer was who's for us.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: appreciate someone who isn't in your group. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person from a different church, or a different way of being Christian than the one you know best, or simply someone outside your circle who does good. The neighbor who runs the food drive. The nurse. Your cousin's church that sings too loudly. Name one good thing they do. Just one, and mean it. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, just say thank you in your head. The bell holds the time.
Not one of us. What John said about the stranger. What Jesus answered: forbid him not.
Your line: not against us, for us. Today, tell someone outside your circle one good thing you've noticed about what they do. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: Salt (Mark 9:42–50)
199.hook: have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another
199.howItsDone: Christians often speak of being "the salt of the earth" and read Mark 9:50 as a call to keep their faith lively and to make peace within the church; many congregations share the peace, a greeting or handshake, during worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John tried to stop a stranger, and heard forbid him not. Your line was not against us, for us. Whose good work did you notice? Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Still in the same house, still talking to the friends who argued about rank, Jesus says some of the hardest-sounding things in Mark. Whoever trips up one of these little ones who believe, it would be better for them to have a millstone hung around their neck and be thrown into the sea. If your hand makes you stumble, cut it off. If your foot, cut it off. If your eye, pluck it out. Better to enter life missing a part than be thrown whole into Gehenna, the valley outside Jerusalem that became a picture of ruin. These sayings are meant to land like a slap. Most Christians have always read them as deliberate exaggeration, not instructions. And then, right at the end, the tone changes, and he talks about something on every kitchen table.
screen: `A MILLSTONE AND THE SEA.` → `CUT IT OFF.` → `SOMETHING ON EVERY TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another." Salt was precious. It kept fish and meat from rotting before refrigerators. It gave taste. In the Hebrew Bible, offerings were seasoned with salt, and there's a phrase, a covenant of salt, for a promise meant to last. Can salt really lose its saltness? Pure salt can't. But much of the salt people used then was gathered from the Dead Sea region, mixed with other minerals. Many explain that damp could wash the true salt out, leaving white stuff that looked like salt and tasted of nothing. Right before this, there's a line nobody is sure about: everyone will be salted with fire. Scholars have puzzled over it for centuries, and Mark doesn't explain it. What is clear is the ending. Have salt in yourselves, and peace with one another. Remember who he's talking to: the men who argued about who's greatest, and shut out the stranger. Keep your taste, your bite, your faith. And then don't use it on each other. That closes this stretch of Mark, the one that kept asking who is this. Washed hands and what comes out of the heart. Crumbs for a mother's daughter. Be opened. Seven baskets. Hard hearts in a boat. Men like trees. You are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. Help my unbelief. Who's the greatest. Not one of us. And salt. Tomorrow the road turns south, toward Jerusalem.
screen: `SALT KEPT THINGS AND GAVE TASTE.` · `SALT THAT LOSES ITS SALTNESS.` · `SALTED WITH FIRE: NOBODY'S SURE.` · `SALT IN YOU, PEACE WITH EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `HAVE SALT IN YOURSELVES, AND HAVE PEACE ONE WITH ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace with one person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you're a little crossways with right now. Not the biggest wound of your life; something smaller. A sharp text. A cold week. A silence that went on too long. Picture them. Keep your salt: you don't have to pretend you were wrong about everything. But ask what one step toward peace would look like. A message. A kind word. Letting it go. If you pray, you can bring them to God by name. The bell holds the time.
Salt. It keeps things and gives them taste. Have salt in yourselves, he says, and have peace one with another.
Your line: salt, and peace. Today, take the one step toward peace you chose, and keep your flavor while you do it. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

200.title: Marriage (Mark 10:1–12)
200.hook: asked about divorce, he points back to creation; churches today apply this in differing ways
200.howItsDone: Many Christian wedding services echo Mark 10:9, that what God has joined no one should put asunder, and many churches pray for married couples during worship; churches differ on divorce and remarriage, from the Catholic Church's annulment process to the Orthodox and many Protestant churches' provisions for remarriage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salt that keeps and gives taste, and the line salt, and peace. Did you take a step toward peace with someone? Day two hundred. And a new stretch of Mark begins: the road to Jerusalem.

Chapter ten, and the road turns south. Jesus leaves Galilee and crosses into Judea and the land beyond the Jordan, and crowds gather again. Some Pharisees come with a question, and Mark tells us it's a test. Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife? It's a live argument in their world. The Law of Moses allowed a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away, and teachers disagreed sharply over what reasons were good enough. Whatever Jesus says, someone will be unhappy. This isn't an abstract question for many of us either. Almost everyone listening knows a marriage that held, and one that broke. So listen closely to where he goes. He doesn't start with the rules. He goes back to the very beginning.
screen: `THE ROAD TURNS SOUTH.` → `IS IT LAWFUL?` → `BACK TO THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: First he asks them: what did Moses command? They answer: Moses allowed a certificate of divorce. And Jesus says Moses wrote that because of the hardness of your hearts. Remember the disciples' hard hearts in the boat, back on day one ninety-one? Mark uses a different Greek word here, but it's the same picture: a heart gone stiff. Then he reaches past Moses to Genesis: from the beginning God made them male and female, and a man shall leave his father and mother, and the two shall be one flesh. And then the line people still hear at weddings, in the King James Bible: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." Asunder means apart. The disciples ask him about it later, in the house, and he goes further: whoever divorces and marries another commits adultery. Notice something unusual. Mark includes a wife divorcing her husband too, which fit Roman law more than the Jewish custom of the day. And notice what divorce often meant then: a woman sent away with a piece of paper, and very often with nothing to live on. Many readers hear in his words a protection for the one most likely to be discarded. Churches apply this passage in different ways, and each takes it seriously. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, and it can declare that a marriage was never valid, an annulment. Orthodox churches hold marriage as lifelong, yet may allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Many Protestant churches allow divorce in some circumstances, such as adultery or abandonment, reading this alongside Matthew and Paul. What they share is the starting point Jesus chose: not the loophole, but the beginning.
screen: `WHAT DID MOSES COMMAND?` · `FOR THE HARDNESS OF YOUR HEART.` · `FROM THE BEGINNING: ONE FLESH.` · `CHURCHES APPLY IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT THEREFORE GOD HATH JOINED TOGETHER, LET NOT MAN PUT ASUNDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one marriage in your mind. Settle, and breathe. It might be your own, your parents', a friend's, a couple just starting, or one that's struggling right now. It might even be one that ended, and the people still living with that. Picture them kindly, both of them. What do they need today? Patience. Time together. Rest. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well, slowly and on purpose. The bell holds the time.
Marriage. Asked about divorce, Jesus answers with the beginning: two becoming one flesh, joined by God.
Your line: what god joined. Today, do one small thing that strengthens a bond you're part of, a marriage, a family, a friendship. Day two hundred.

201.title: Let the children come (Mark 10:13–16)
201.hook: the disciples shoo away children, and he's indignant
201.howItsDone: Many churches that baptize infants read this passage at baptisms, and churches that baptize believers often read it at services where parents present a baby for dedication and blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard question about divorce, answered from the beginning. Your line was what god joined. Which bond did you strengthen? Day two hundred one.

If you've ever taken a small child somewhere important, you know the look. The one from the person at the desk who's hoping you'll keep the little one quiet and out of the way. Now it's the disciples wearing that look. Parents are bringing their little children to Jesus, just so he'll touch them, lay a hand on their heads. And the disciples step in and send them off. He's busy. He's important. There's a serious conversation going on about divorce and the Law. Take the kids home. And Mark tells us something he tells us nowhere else. When Jesus saw it, he was angry. Not with the parents. Not with the children. With his friends.
screen: `PARENTS BRING THEIR LITTLE ONES.` → `THE DISCIPLES SEND THEM OFF.` → `AND HE'S ANGRY.`

segments.voice: The King James says he was much displeased. The Greek word is stronger: indignant, properly annoyed. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and both leave that part out. Mark keeps it. Then come the words: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in 1611 English, meant allow. Let them come. Don't stop them. And then the line that turns it into a lesson for the grown-ups: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will not enter it. How does a little child receive something? Watch a toddler handed a cookie. There's no negotiating, no asking what's the catch, no working out whether they've earned it. Hands open, and it's theirs. Children then had no standing and nothing to trade. That's the point. The kingdom isn't a prize for the deserving. It's a gift for people who know how to receive one. Mark ends the scene with three verbs: he took them up in his arms, put his hands on them, and blessed them. Not a pat on the head from a distance. Churches read this passage in different settings. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many Reformed churches baptize infants, and this is one of the passages they often read at a baptism. Baptist and many other churches baptize those old enough to profess faith, and often read it when parents bring a baby to be dedicated and blessed. Either way, the children end up in his arms.
screen: `MARK ALONE SAYS HE WAS ANGRY.` · `SUFFER MEANS ALLOW.` · `RECEIVE IT LIKE A CHILD.` · `ARMS, HANDS, BLESSING.` · then, large: `FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive something the way a child would. Settle, and breathe. Notice one thing you've been given today that you didn't earn. The breath you're taking right now. Sunlight. A message from someone. Your own hands. Don't analyze it. Don't ask whether you deserve it. Just take it, the way a toddler takes a cookie, with open hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you, like a child would. The bell holds the time.
Let the children come. His angry defense of the little ones, and his lesson: receive the kingdom as a child receives a gift.
Your line: like a child. Today, when someone gives you something, a compliment, help, a gift, don't deflect it. Just say thank you. Day two hundred one.

202.title: The rich young man (Mark 10:17–22)
202.hook: Jesus looked at him and loved him, then asked for everything
202.howItsDone: Some Christians, especially in monastic orders, take vows of poverty inspired by this story; many others read it as a call to examine what holds them back, and to give generously to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples shooed the children away, and he took them in his arms. Your line was like a child. Did you receive something without deflecting it? Day two hundred two.

Jesus is setting out on the road again when a man comes running up. Grown men didn't run much in that world; it wasn't dignified. This one runs, and kneels in the dust, and asks the biggest question there is. "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" Jesus pushes back on the compliment first: why call me good? No one is good but God alone. Then he lists the commandments everybody knows. Don't kill, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't defraud, honor your father and mother. And the man says, sincerely, I've kept all these since I was young. He isn't boasting. He's a good man. And he still feels something's missing, or he wouldn't have run.
screen: `A MAN COMES RUNNING.` → `WHAT SHALL I DO?` → `I'VE KEPT THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me." Look at the order. First he looks at him. Then he loves him. Only then does he ask the hardest thing. Mark is the only gospel that says Jesus loved him. Matthew and Luke tell the story and leave it out. And by the way, Mark never says he was young. Matthew calls him a young man, and Luke calls him a ruler. Our title stitches the Gospels together. Then the saddest line: "And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." He doesn't argue. He doesn't sneer. He just can't do it, and walks away sad. And Jesus lets him go. What happened to him after? The Gospels are silent. Christians read the command in more than one way. Some have taken it literally: the early monk Anthony of Egypt, the story goes, heard this read in church and gave away his family's land. Many others read it as aimed at this one man, and at whatever holds any of us back from following. Almost everyone notices the love. The hard word wasn't a rejection. It came from someone who had looked at him closely and loved what he saw.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look before you advise. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'd like to tell something to. Advice, a correction, a hard truth. Before any of that, just look at them in your mind. Their face. What they're carrying. What they're good at. Stay there until you feel something like love for them, even a little. If you pray, you can ask to see them the way Jesus looked at the man. Only then, if you still need to, decide what you'd say. The bell holds the time.
The rich young man. A good man who ran to Jesus, was loved, was asked for everything, and walked away sad.
Your line: he loved him. Today, before you give anyone advice, look at them first, long enough to love them. Day two hundred two.

203.title: A camel and a needle (Mark 10:23–31)
203.hook: with people it's impossible, but not with God
203.howItsDone: Christians often turn to this passage when talking about money and generosity; many give a regular share of their income to church and charity, and some traditions encourage giving away something valued, especially in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a good man ran to Jesus, and walked away sad. Your line was he loved him. Did you look at someone long enough to love them first? Day two hundred three. The end of the week.

The man with great possessions is still walking away down the road, and Jesus watches him go. Then he turns and looks around at his friends. In the King James Bible: "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" The disciples are stunned. In their world, wealth often looked like God's blessing. If the rich can't get in, who can? He says it again, more gently, calling them children. And then he reaches for the most ridiculous picture he can find. The biggest animal anyone in Galilee knew. The smallest hole anyone had ever threaded. It's the kind of thing you'd say to make someone laugh out loud, and then go very quiet.
screen: `HE WATCHES THE MAN GO.` → `HOW HARDLY SHALL THEY.` → `THE BIGGEST AND THE SMALLEST.`

segments.voice: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God." People have tried hard to make this easier. You may have heard that there was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called the Eye of the Needle, where a camel had to kneel and squeeze through. It's a lovely sermon illustration, but there's no evidence such a gate existed in Jesus's day; the story shows up many centuries later. Others noticed that the Greek for camel, kamēlos, is one letter from kamilos, a rope, and a few later copies say rope. But the oldest manuscripts say camel. He meant impossible. The disciples hear it that way too: then who can be saved? And Jesus looks at them and says: "With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible." The camel isn't squeezing through by trying harder. Something only God can do. Peter blurts out: we've left everything to follow you. And Jesus promises that nobody who has left home and family for his sake will miss out; they'll receive a hundred times over, homes and brothers and sisters and mothers, now.
